title: Bond Sports Round 2
block_types_note: Built from Ginsberg_BondSports_Round2_Workbook.html (text verbatim), using only block types already live in prod: the SaaS word list is one text note per term (label = the word), the competitor table is one list per competitor (Built for / What it does), and the 10-lead table is ten short answer boxes, Lead 1 to Lead 10.

blocks.body: You're meeting Marc for sure, and maybe Matt too. They're the two people who started Bond. Learn both names and faces from LinkedIn before tomorrow.

blocks.title: Marc Rothschild · Co-founder and President
items: Started a company called Selectable Media with Matt and ran its day to day operations.
A big media company, Meredith, bought Selectable Media in 2015. Marc then ran digital revenue at Meredith: the sales team, client services, and influencer marketing.
Then became President and COO at Clique, the company behind the Who What Wear brand.
Also worked at AOL earlier on.
What it means for you: he has built and run sales teams. Expect questions about how you think about selling.

blocks.title: Matt Minoff · Co-founder and CEO
items: Captain of the Yale men's basketball team, then played professionally in Israel.
Ran Selectable Media as CEO, then was Chief Digital Officer at Meredith.
Why he started Bond: he organized a lot of games and tournaments and kept getting frustrated by how hard it was to find and book places to play.
Matt is the one who passed your email to Andy.

blocks.title: If both of them are there
blocks.body:
Answer the person who asked, but look at both of them.

If Matt is there, thank him in one line and move on: "Thanks again for passing my email along to Andy."

Thank you notes go to both, separately, the same day.
Your notes on Marc and Matt
Anything you find on their LinkedIn or in recent Bond posts. Something they shared, a school, a sport, a post.

blocks.label: Your notes on Marc and Matt
What Bond does
blocks.body: Bond sells software that runs a sports facility. Booking, sign ups, payments, and memberships, all in one place.
Picture a hockey rink using one app to book ice time, another for league sign ups, another for payments, and a spreadsheet for memberships. Bond replaces all of that with one system.
Who pays: the facility owner. Families just use it to book and pay.

blocks.label: Who they sell to
blocks.body: Ice rinks, indoor soccer, baseball and softball, basketball, volleyball, multi sport complexes, parks and rec departments, and colleges.

blocks.title: Big customers to know
items: Black Bear Sports Group: the biggest owner of ice rinks in the U.S. Bond runs all 36 of their rinks, 34 youth hockey clubs, and 4 leagues. Five year deal.
TOCA Football: big soccer brand. Bond runs their sign ups.
Socceroof: indoor soccer. Dropped their own system for Bond and grew from six to ten facilities.
Chelsea Piers: invoiced over $1M in one tryout day on Bond.
Yale: runs its campus rec facilities on Bond.

blocks.title: New things Bond launched
items: Bond ID: a digital pass on your phone. One tap to check in instead of waiting at the front desk.
SUB-ZERO partnership: Bond now talks to rink maintenance software, so the scheduling team and the ice crew stay in sync.
Online booking: customers can book fields, lessons, and parties 24/7 without calling. Socceroof was the first soccer company to use it.

blocks.title: The money (Bond is private, so these are labeled)
items: $250M+ a year in registrations: from Bond's website. This is NOT Bond's revenue. It's the money families pay facilities that runs through Bond.
About $4.8M in revenue: an outside estimate. Rough guess only.
About 30 to 40 employees. Small company.
Investors: Rally Ventures led, with Correlation Ventures. Funding totals don't match across sources, so don't quote a number.

What it means for you: Bond runs on investor money, and investors want growth. Growth means new customers. New customers start with SDRs booking meetings. Your job sits at the very start of how Bond grows.

blocks.body: You don't need to use these words to sound smart. You just need to understand them when Marc or Matt does.

blocks.label: SaaS (software as a service)
blocks.body: Software you rent monthly or yearly instead of buying once. Facilities pay Bond a subscription.

blocks.label: Vertical SaaS
blocks.body: Software built for one industry. Bond is software built just for sports facilities.

blocks.label: SaaS+ (payments)
blocks.body: The software makes money twice: from the subscription and from payments that run through it. Rally Ventures said it plans to work with Bond on payments and other add on products.

blocks.label: ARR / MRR
blocks.body: Annual or monthly recurring revenue. The subscription money that comes in every year or month.

blocks.label: Churn
blocks.body: Customers who cancel. Low churn means people stay.

blocks.label: Lead
blocks.body: A facility that might be a fit.

blocks.label: Prospect
blocks.body: A lead you're actively reaching out to.

blocks.label: Qualified lead
blocks.body: A lead that's a real fit: right size, has budget, and is open to switching.

blocks.label: Inbound / outbound
blocks.body: Inbound: they come to you, like a demo request on the website. Outbound: you reach out first, like a cold call or email.

blocks.label: Cadence (or sequence)
blocks.body: A planned run of calls, emails, and messages to one prospect over a few weeks.

blocks.label: Pipeline
blocks.body: Every deal in progress, from first call to signed.

blocks.label: Demo
blocks.body: A meeting where the facility sees how Bond works.

blocks.label: SDR (your job)
blocks.body: Finds prospects and books the meeting.

blocks.label: AE (account executive)
blocks.body: Runs the demo and closes the deal.

blocks.label: Quota
blocks.body: The number you're expected to hit each month or quarter, like meetings booked.

blocks.label: CRM
blocks.body: The system where every call, email, and lead gets tracked.

blocks.label: Implementation (onboarding)
blocks.body: Setting a new customer up on Bond. Bond says about 3 to 4 weeks.

blocks.label: Upsell
blocks.body: Selling more to a customer you already have, like adding a new location.

blocks.body: You don't need to be a software expert. You need to know who else is out there and what makes Bond different.

blocks.title: SportsEngine (NBC)
items: Built for: Youth leagues, clubs, volunteer run organizations
What it does: Sign ups, payments, rosters, schedules, team app, websites, tournaments

blocks.title: LeagueApps
items: Built for: Youth and local sports clubs, leagues, camps, parks
What it does: Sign ups, payments, scheduling, websites. Calls itself "the operating system and community for youth and local sports leaders."

blocks.title: Upper Hand
items: Built for: Training facilities, academies, coaches, camps
What it does: Scheduling, memberships, payments. Its pitch: "No more juggling tools." Plans start at $79 a month.

blocks.title: DaySmart Recreation
items: Built for: Ice and skating rinks, skating schools
What it does: Scheduling, mobile booking, 60+ reports, Learn to Skate USA partnership

blocks.title: EZFacility
items: Built for: Sports and fitness facilities
What it does: Facility scheduling and memberships

blocks.title: What makes Bond different (from Bond's own site)
items: Built for big, complex facilities. Multi sport complexes and ice rinks, not just youth clubs. Proof: Black Bear runs all 36 rinks on Bond.
Everything actually connects. Scheduling, sign ups, payments, and reporting share the same information, so staff stop copying things between systems. Move one event and everything updates.
Fast to switch. Live in about 3 to 4 weeks. Bond moves the data and trains the staff, and the facility keeps running the whole time.
Constantly improving. New features every week.
Real people for support. By phone, text, or email.

blocks.title: Coaching notes
blocks.body:
Upper Hand also says "one system," so "all in one" alone isn't the difference. Bond's real edge is how big and complicated the facilities are that it can run.

Never trash a competitor. Just say what each one is built for.
"Why Bond over the competition?"

blocks.title: Answer starter
blocks.body: "A lot of the other options are built for clubs and leagues, or for one sport. Bond is built for the facility itself, especially the big multi sport ones and rinks, and everything runs in one system. Black Bear running 36 rinks on it says a lot."

blocks.body: Phone screens at 18

blocks.title: Answer starter
blocks.body: "My first real job was at my mom's recruiting firm. I started when I was 18, doing phone screens with candidates, and a lot of them had been working longer than I'd been alive."
Caribbean Baseball Organization

blocks.title: Answer starter
blocks.body: "I was filling a summer league roster, calling, texting, and emailing high school and college players and their parents, and following up until they signed. We got to over 50 players. I liked seeing my work actually make a difference."
The Padres

blocks.title: Answer starter
blocks.body: "I'm on the event operations team at Petco Park. They picked me to start training new hires, so I help get new crew ready for game days. I love the people I work with."
Dalsimer Atlas

blocks.title: Answer starter
blocks.body: "In high school I worked weekends for Dalsimer Atlas, an event company in Boca, setting up and tearing down really high end parties. It was a lot of manual work, but everything had to be perfect, and I was dealing with clients and vendors the whole time."

blocks.text: Not taking no for an answer

blocks.body: Breaking into MLB

blocks.title: Answer starter
blocks.body:
"Getting into MLB was rough. Starting my sophomore year, I was applying for internships, calling, emailing, messaging people on LinkedIn. I thought I had a really good resume and was doing everything right. But I got rejected a lot, and mostly I just got ghosted. That was frustrating. But it made me figure out better ways to get noticed. It took about two years.

What finally worked was I stopped chasing job postings and started way earlier, just trying to make any connection I could. Eventually I connected with the Director of Events at the Padres, months before applications opened. I stayed in touch, applied the day it posted, and let her know. I got the interview, and it was a Zoom with three managers and seven candidates all at once, which was kind of wild. But I got the job. So I packed up and moved to San Diego by myself."
End on the move to San Diego and stop. Don't explain what it says about you.

sections.title: How You Used AI to Prepare

blocks.body: The job posting asks for someone who will "leverage technology and data to consistently improve outreach." Say plainly how you used AI. It's part of how you work.
How you prepared for today

blocks.title: Answer starter
blocks.body: "I used AI a lot to prepare for today. It helped me research Bond and your competitors, build my lead list, and figure out what to ask your customers. Then I made the calls myself and checked everything. I see it the same way for this job. It gets me prepared faster so I can spend more time actually talking to people."
Be ready: "How do you use AI day to day?"
